ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.contribution: Required first-year development in scholarly argument, writing and reflective practice.
ACCPPDE101.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI

BENBUSI211.name: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
BENBUSI211.contribution: As we enter the “Age of AI,” this course explores AI’s business, managerial, economic, and societal implications. It is designed for UCR students with a strong interest in AI and requires no prior technical background. The course traces AI’s evolution from early research to generative AI, highlighting its capabilities and limits. Through real-world examples and business cases, students analyse AI’s impact on competitiveness, innovation, labour markets, economic growth, inequality, climate change and society. In this context, students critically examine AI governance and ethics, addressing issues such as bias, privacy, and fairness across business functions (e.g. Marketing, HR, Finance), while also exploring corporate governance and regulation more broadly. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
BENBUSI211.topics: AI capabilities and limitations; AI in business functions and industries; Agentic AI; Market structure and business models; Automation and augmentation; Labour markets and productivity; Innovation and economic growth; Inequality; Techno-economic paradigms and economic narratives; AI ethics and societal impacts; Corporate governance and AI regulation; National AI readiness and industrial policy; Future AI scenarios

DISARIN111.name: AI Ethics
DISARIN111.contribution: Developments in AI are transforming the nature of human interaction and raising fundamental questions concerning human flourishing and its alignment with technological progress. This course examines these issues from both philosophical and psychological pe rspectives, while exploring the deep connections between the two fields. In a module on the ethics of AI, we'll consider ramifications of the use of AI in the context of moral inquiry. Core topics include AI fairness and bias , privacy, responsibility and accountability . We will also approach the question concerning the moral status of AI systems , and some of the broader implications of AI, focusing on existential risks and broad political implications of the use of AI. In a module on psychology of AI, we will examine what it means to be human when AI systems increasingly mirror or simulate uniquely human capabilities. Research shows that people may both over-trust and resist AI in decision-making, which subsequently raises questions on responsibility and agency. In clinical and therapeutic contexts, AI challenges ideas of empathy, confidentiality, and the therapeutic alliance, while in organisational and social domains, algorithmic biases reflect and amplify existing stereotypes. Developmentally, AI companions and tutors shape how children learn and relate, prompting concerns about attachment and socialisation. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
DISARIN111.topics: Algorithmic fairness and bias; Privacy and surveillance; Responsibility and accountability; Human-value alignment; Moral status of AI; Existential risk and democratic implications; Trust and agency in human-AI interaction; AI in clinical care; Child development and AI; Social and organizational effects of AI; AI in forensic psychology; Cognitive and socioemotional development; AI consciousness and sentience

DISCOMP212.name: Database Management Systems
DISCOMP212.contribution: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
DISCOMP212.topics: Introduces relational database management systems and SQL. Covers relational database theory, authorization, normalization and query processing.

DISDATA111.name: Introduction to Data Science
DISDATA111.contribution: Data science provides tools for extracting meaningful information from data. In this course, you develop foundational abilities in data visualization as well as data cleaning and manipulation. Next to traditional data coming in the form of tables, we explore non-traditional data types such as spatial data and text data. The course includes much hands -on work with example data sets coming from sciences, social sciences, and arts and humanities. At the end of the course, you carry out your own research project in which you apply your data analysis and visualization skills to answer a research question. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
DISDATA111.topics: Data visualization; Exploratory data analysis; Tidy data; Data transformation and integration; Dates and times; Web data; Text data; Geospatial data; Programming functions; Data-based research questions

DISDATA211.name: Machine Learning
DISDATA211.contribution: Machine learning concerns an ever -expanding set of tools for understanding data and making predictions. This course introduces the fundamentals of machine learning. It presents several of the most important modelling and prediction techniques, along with several relevant applications. Topics include linear regression, classification, resampling methods, shrinkage approaches, tree - based methods, support vector machines, clustering, and more. Real-world examples are used to illustrate the methods, their strengths, and their limitations. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
DISDATA211.topics: Prediction and model accuracy; Regression and classification; Resampling and validation; Model selection and regularization; High-dimensional data; Nonlinear regression; Tree-based learning; Support vector methods; Dimension reduction; Unsupervised learning; Feature engineering

DISDATA311.name: Neural Networks & Deep Learning
DISDATA311.contribution: Neural networks have enabled major advances in areas such as computer vision, large language models, and generative AI. This course focuses on the underlying theory as well as practical implementations in the Python programming language using packages such as TensorFlow . No familiarity with Python is assumed, but a willingness to learn and write code in Python is essential. In the first part of the course, w e start by building and training our own basic neural networks from scratch. We also use TensorFlow to create bigger networks and apply them to tabular data. In the second part of the course, we move on to more complex neural networks for applications such as computer vision and text classification . We also discuss recent developments in large language models (such as ChatGPT) . Finally, if time per mits, we have a brief look at image generation models (such as DALL-E). Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
DISDATA311.topics: Perceptrons and ADALINE; Multilayer neural networks; Gradient descent and backpropagation; Bias-variance trade-off and regularization; Computation graphs; Network architectures and interpretation; Computer vision; Time-series learning; Text classification and generation; Transformers and large language models; Feature engineering; Predictive performance

DISGATE102.name: Mathematical Methods
DISGATE102.contribution: Mathematics is the language used to grasp understanding of, to explore, and to gain insight in any of the sciences: physics, chemistry, biology, as well as engineering. None of these can be well understood or appreciated without sufficient skills in mathematics. The aim of this introductory course in the mathematics track is to learn basic widely-used mathematical techniques, such as differentiation, various techniques for integration, complex numbers and differential equations. These techniques are put into context in projects related to real situations in the fields of physics, chemistry, biology, economics, sociology, etc. In this course students will continue to construct knowledge on their mathematical bases already founded. Students will solve many problems as homework assignments. Furthermore, two exams will assess the students for their level of understanding and their ability to solve relevant mathematical problems. A lot of class time will be used to solve and discuss textbook problems. 3 Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
DISGATE102.topics: Functions and limits; Continuity; Differentiation; Optimization; Taylor series; Complex numbers; Definite and indefinite integrals; Integration techniques; First-order differential equations; Population-growth and predator–prey models; Second-order linear differential equations; Dynamic models

ENSDELT211.name: Living with Water
ENSDELT211.contribution: Delta regions around the world face growing challenges related to sea-level rise, flooding, freshwater scarcity, land subsidence, and unequal access to water and protection. At the same time, these regions are home to millions of people whose lives are shaped by water. This course explores how societies in delta regions manage water risks and opportunities, with a particular focus on the Dutch province of Zeeland as a living laboratory. Students are introduced to key concepts in sustainable water management, including flood protection, drainage and freshwater management, salinization, land subsidence, the ecological consequences of water infrastructure, and the social dimensions of water governance. The course examines how historical events have shaped contemporary approaches to water management, and how governance structures, laws, and institutions influence decisions about safety, land use, sustainability, and whose interests are prioritized. Throughout the course, emphasis is placed on the idea of adapting to water dynamics through integrated strategies, nature-based solutions, and resilient planning, while critically reflecting on questions of long-term social impacts. Learning takes place through a combination of assigned readings, short lectures, group discussions, and in-class activities that encourage critical reflection and collaborative learning. Students engage with real-world cases through guest speakers from policy and research, as well as excursions and field-based activities in Zeeland when possible. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
ENSDELT211.topics: Delta environments; Flood risk and protection; Drainage and freshwater management; Sea-level rise and subsidence; Salinization; Water infrastructure and ecological consequences; Water governance, law and justice; Contaminants and pollution; EU Water Framework Directive; Nature-based adaptation; Urban ecology and water; Long-term delta resilience

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.contribution: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions. The first part of this course introduces you to the basic conceptual tools for understanding governance and to the major fault line in tackling sustainability problems as identified by Charles Mann in “The Wizard and the Prophet”. Wizards are techno-optimists who believe humanity’s creativity can tackle every challenge, whilst Prophets argue that humans should take a holistic and systemic approach that calls for a drastic reduction of exploiting the earth resources to respect planetary boundaries. In the second part of the course, we use Problem Based Learning to examine governance solutions to concrete sustainability challenges regarding food, freshwater, energy, and climate change. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
ENSDELT312.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility

ENSENVI311.name: Environmental Biogeochemistry
ENSENVI311.contribution: This course focusses on the biogeochemical processes on the earths surface. Most are related to soil-mineral-rock water interactions under near Earth -surface conditions. Biological and chemical controls on mineral formation processes will be studied in further detail as well as adsorption and leaching of nutrients or metals. Furthermore, (waste) -water treatment and engineered processes to recover valuable resources from waste, as well as some anthropogenic resource cycles are topics of this course. The theoretical and practical knowledge taught in SCIEART201/202 will be supplemented by using advanced geochemical modeling tools such as G eochemist Workbench. This course is very suitable for students in chemistry, geology and environmental science. The course may include some simple lab experiments, furthermore (in-class) exercises, one quiz and a case study. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
ENSENVI311.topics: Natural-water composition; Chemical equilibrium and ionic activity; Aqueous speciation and complexation; Mineral saturation, precipitation and dissolution; Carbonate equilibria, alkalinity and buffering; Ocean acidification; Redox processes and microbial controls; Adsorption and mineral surfaces; Weathering and clay formation; Biomineralization; Contaminant transport; Environmental remediation and resource recovery

ENSGATE101.name: Sustainability Essentials I
ENSGATE101.contribution: ENSGATE101 - Sustainability Essentials serves as the Gateway course to all 200 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy all 200 level course in the cluster. We will use the model of planetary boundaries to discuss the concepts of sustainability with an anthropogenic focus. The planetary boundaries concept was presented in 2009 and provides a novel synthesis of the most pertinent global environmental challenges by analysing the risk of crossing critical thresholds in the behaviour of the Earth system’s processes. These boundaries act as a framework to define a "safe operating space for humanity," highlighting the limits within which human development can occur without causing catastrophic harm to the planet. 3 Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
ENSGATE101.topics: Planetary boundaries and the Anthropocene; Exponential growth and environmental change; Graphs, rates and uncertainty; Dynamic systems; Chemical bonds, reactions and equilibria; Ocean acidification and nutrient cycles; Thermodynamics and entropy; Greenhouse gases and energy; Ozone depletion; Newtonian mechanics, stress and strain; Biopolymers and material properties

ENSGATE201.name: Sustainability Essentials II
ENSGATE201.contribution: ENSGATE201 - Sustainability Essentials II serves as the Gateway course to several 300 level courses in the Environment and Sustainability Cluster. For that purpose we will discuss the tools and knowledge you need to follow and enjoy these course in the cluster. We will focus on three main topics (Waves, Chemistry and Material science) and on how they relate to Sustainability. You will have the opportunity to explore the topics in individual reflective journals as well as a project at the end of the course. In the project, you will use what you learned to analyse and discuss green washing. 3 Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
ENSGATE201.topics: Electromagnetic and mechanical waves; Wave composition and interference; Optical spectroscopy; Electron microscopy; Inorganic and organic chemistry; Chemical testing; Material structure and crystallography; Stress and strain; Sustainable material design; Geological wave applications; Nuclear power and waste; Greenwashing

ENSSUST111.name: Climate Change
ENSSUST111.contribution: Climate change is the defining challenge of our time. It has large impacts on both the living and non-living Earth systems, as well as drives a number of profound societal transformations. This course is roughly divided in 3 parts. First, we will first focus on the drivers of anthropogenic climate change and its impacts on the natural world. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) the properties of greenhouse gases, sea level rise, ocean acidification, climate feedback loops and effects on various biome types. Secondly, we will discuss impacts on various aspects of society. Topics discussed include (but are not limited to) food production, transportation, construction, health, and migration patterns. We will discuss climate governance and -justice. We will also look at the history of the climate change debate and identify strategies that have been deployed by interest groups to sow doubt and misinformation. Lastly, we will look into solutions for both adaptation and mitigation, such as renewable energy systems, carbon dioxide storage and climate-adaptive spatial planning. The course will include a number of guest lectures and excursions. After taking the course, you will be able to explain the fundamentals of climate change science. You will also be able to navigate a vast flow of information on climate change, and identify main and reliable sources; you will have insight in main climate change issues and have an overview of the pathways to mitigation and adaptation. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
ENSSUST111.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation

ENSSUST112.name: Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy
ENSSUST112.contribution: To prepare our society for a circular and sustainable future, we need to evaluate the environmental impact of products, processes, or services throughout their entire lifecycle, from raw material extraction to final disposal, or ideally re-usage as new raw materials. To do this, we have to understand the environmental, social and health consequences of products and processes and develop a strategic planning for future activi- ties. ENSSUST112 - Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economywill be heavily focussed on “learning by doing”, rather than by just studying books. Therefore most of this course will consist of analysing different products, processes and services and include guest lectures by experts working in the field of sustainability and circularity. 3 Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
ENSSUST112.topics: Circular economy; Product and process life cycles; Resource extraction and reuse; Environmental impacts; Social and health consequences; Life-cycle management strategies; Product-based and process-based assessment; Costs and revenues; Sustainable product and process planning

ENSSUST313.name: Research in a Sustainable Delta
ENSSUST313.contribution: In this project course you will work in small teams of two or three students on a research problem relevant for sustainability in the broadest sense. We are looking for collaborations with local companies and other institutions. The research questions are supplied by a regional institution or company that is active in areas related to sustainability in the broadest sense. In this way it is guaranteed that the research projects are indeed relevant for the Zeeland delta. Furthermore, students will have access to expertise and/or facilities of the external partner, which will broaden their perspective. Usually, there will be one person affiliated with the external partner organization involved with a project team as external advisor. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
ENSSUST313.topics: Regionally situated sustainability problems; Research-question development; Research planning; Academic literature and evidence; External stakeholder collaboration; Applied sustainability investigation

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.contribution: This course offers three different perspectives on the law: the legal, the social and the normative. We spend the first part of the course exploring the definitions of law and the different understandings of law in a general sense. We take a brief look at the different legal systems of the world, and we discuss various fields of law: constitutional law, administrative law, criminal law, international law and human rights, as well as select fields of private law including property law, contract and torts law. After the Fall break, students consider the relationships between law and society and the concept of justice. In addition to reading and discussing the main principles within each field of law, we explore these through reading case law and performing trial simulations. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSGATE102.topics: Legal positivism and empirical and normative perspectives; Common-law and civil-law traditions; Constitutional and administrative law; Criminal law; International law and human rights; Property, contract and tort law; Justice; Law and social control; Law and social change; Race and gender in law; Family law

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.contribution: This course gives a chronological overview of history in the modern period (1815-2025). The nineteenth century saw the rise of industrial societies and of the new political ideals of popular sovereignty (e.g. Marxism, socialism) and national self-determination. These forces continued to operate in the twentieth century, which was characterized by tremendous upheavals like the Russian Revolution, the two World Wars and the demise of communism in Eastern Europe. The course offers a survey of the main economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present. Special attention will be paid to the relationship between economic developments and the international changes of the Balance of Power. A number of issues of seminal importance to modern history will be analysed thoroughly: the revolutions of the 19th century, the Belle Epoque, the origins of the First World War, the Great Depression, and the Second World War, the Cold War and the rise of the welfare state, the decolonization process, and the European economic and monetary co-operation between nations. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSHIST111.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future

GOSHIST213.name: Ways of War
GOSHIST213.contribution: This course gives a chronological overview of the history of Warfare in the Western World from antiquity to the present day. All aspects of war on land, sea, and in the air are covered: weapons and technology; strategy and tactics; discipline and intelligence; mercenaries and standing armies; cavalry and infantry; chivalry and Blitzkrieg; guerrilla assault and nuclear arsenals. The central controversial thesis of this course is that war in western societies has followed a unique path leading to the Western hegemony of the world. From Greek hoplites, Roman legionnaires to the jet plane and cruise missile, war has served as the driving force behind the West’s rise to global domination. The history of the West, both at home and overseas, has centred around ferocious competition for mastery among uncompromisingly ambitious powers, in which the ruthless, innovative, and the decisive displaced the complacent, the imitative, and the irresolute. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSHIST213.topics: Western warfare and global power; Ancient infantry and Roman warfare; Medieval warfare; Gunpowder and naval warfare; Overseas conquest; Dynastic and national warfare; Industrialization of war; World wars; Cold War and nuclear strategy; Guerrilla warfare and terrorism; Military leadership; Soldiers' experience, morale and cohesion; Future warfare

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.contribution: This Social and Cultural History course (the study of people and their expressions) introduces Native American histories and life from the 19th through the 21st century. Throughout the term we work with Indigenous students, professors, experts, and elders to explore topics including the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s, human trafficking, Traditional Ecological Knowledge (TEK) and cultural resistance and regeneration that play out in language revival, food ways, and Indigenous music, art, and film. Our readings, activities and conversations draw from Indigenous methodologies that center storytelling, respect, and reciprocity. We also draw from Indigenous understanding of knowledge as relational, embodied and practiced rather than abstract, extractive, and memorized. An example is the activist artwork at the center of our first collaboration. It is crafted collectively, mobile, and sustained through relationships over time, rather than something that is created by one person into a finished product that is owned by another person. The fields of gender studies, psychology and sociology help us understand the presence of the past in Native American history and life, especially when we explore childhood, migration, trauma, and family matters. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSHIST311.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.contribution: Develops historical inquiry into the American Century through research questions, critical engagement with sources and a substantial research paper.
GOSHIST312.topics: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

GOSLAWJ212.name: Introduction to Public International Law
GOSLAWJ212.contribution: This course serves as a general introduction to public international law as a field of study and professional discipline. Designed to provide you with a foundational knowledge of the creation and the historical evolution of the subject, it is broadly divided into three parts. The first part deals with general principles of international law such as its sources, subjects, and organization. In the second part, the focus shifts to specific domains, namely the regulation of the use of force, the law of armed co nflict, international criminal law, refugee law, and environmental law. The final part addresses the politics of international law as it delves into issues such as the right to self-determination, Third World Approaches to International Law, and questions of treaty negotiation, compliance and effectiveness. The general purpose of the course is to shed light on some of the most important questions of international law both from a formal legal and a social science perspective. Performance in the course will be assessed through in-class exercises, a preparatory and an open book exam, a podcast and a reflection report. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSLAWJ212.topics: Sources and theories of international law; Treaty law; International legal subjects; Jurisdiction and immunities; Domestic courts and international law; State responsibility; Use of force; UN reform; Armed conflict and international criminal law; International human rights and economic law; Environmental law; Self-determination; Third World Approaches to International Law; Soft law, compliance and effectiveness; Global environmental treaties

GOSLAWJ312.name: Foundations of European Union Law
GOSLAWJ312.contribution: EU law is everywhere, from the very strict new rules on data-protection that literally pop-up with every website you open, to less apparent instances such as the EU rules on reducing plastic bags that have found their way into distinct and different national laws throughout the EU. European law by now significantly affects the legal order in European countries and reflects as well as shapes the process of European integration in multiple ways. This course introduces you to the EU legal order by familiarizing you first with the institutional framework of the European Union and the organization of its legal foundations in particular. We will then survey the key substantive areas of EU law that revolve around EU fundamental rights, citizenship, and the freedom of movement of persons, workers, goods and establishments. You will be equipped to understand the EU legal order and research its manifestations both at the EU level as well as in the domestic context in which most of the EU law manifests itself in the lives of citizens, consumers, businesses and governments. There will also be guest lectures to further illustrate EU law and its functioning in theory and practice. The course is divided in two main parts. In the first part we will jointly examine the procedural aspects of EU law through a combination of brief lectures, in-class exercises and discussions. In the second part we will study the substantive law of the EU through the method of Problem Based Learning. Students will study a relevant case using the seven-step PBL method. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSLAWJ312.topics: European integration and institutions; EU legal sources and fundamental rights; Competences, subsidiarity and proportionality; Supremacy; Direct and indirect effect; State liability; Preliminary rulings; Review of EU acts and enforcement; EU citizenship; Free movement of persons, workers and goods; Establishment and services; Digital-market regulation and green transition

GOSPHIL111.name: Introduction to Western Philosophy
GOSPHIL111.contribution: Philosophy asks the most fundamental questions about the ways we think and act—about, amongst other things, the nature of knowledge, consciousness, our responsibilities towards others, freedom, the existence of god, whether and in what sense our lives can be said to have meaning. Philosophical questions might appear to be simple at first glance, and many of us would have immediate intuitive responses to at least some of them. But providing coherent, lucid, and compelling responses to philosophical questions is a very challenging endeavor. This course introduces central themes from the Western philosophical tradition, spanning 2,500 years of history from the ancient Greeks to cutting-edge work from our own time. We will become familiar with the issues discussed by philosophers, inquire into their significance and their relation to thought in other disciplines, such as psychology, law, physics, computer science, and political science. And, even more importantly, we will acquaint ourselves with theoretical methods and tools that have been used by philosophers to support their conclusions and ideas. 3 Through detailed engagement with central philosophical ideas and arguments, we will develop a critical perspective and approach the rewarding task of articulating our own views on philosophical issues. We shall see that philosophy is a paradigmatic exercise in critical reasoning: it provides an opportunity to develop reasoning skills through rigorous and precise argumentation concerning issues of great importance to our lives. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSPHIL111.topics: Knowledge, opinion and scepticism; Virtue, duty and consequentialist ethics; Moral objectivity; Existence of God; Idealism and causation; Mind-body problem and consciousness; AI and consciousness; Free will and responsibility; Personal identity and non-self; Existentialism; Race and gender; Time; Meaning of life

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.contribution: Our actions and decisions are structured by the ways we think about values, about what the good is. This course explores theories of moral reasoning, building upon historical and contemporary sources. In the first part of the course, we will examine the main theories in ethics – virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism – as well as questions pertaining to moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility, feminist contributions to ethical theory, the challenge of nihilism, and the relation of happiness and pleasure to ethics. The second part of the course largely focuses on practical ethics, touching upon topics such as equality, animal rights, poverty and wealth, future generations, climate change, historical injustice. We will examine our attitudes to these contentious and challenging issues, the way the topics relate to each other, and the manner in which questions in practical ethics highlight and bring into focus broader concerns pertaining to moral, political, and legal theory. Students taking the course will acquire in-depth knowledge of ethical theories, to be assessed through a mid-term exam. They will also work on developing research skills in papers and presentations, analyzing and assessing arguments from ethical theory and practical ethics while articulating an independent, informed perspective. Towards that end, throughout the term students will compose two reflection papers concerning topics in ethics, and in the second part of the term students will develop a research project comprising a final argumentative essay and a presentation. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSPHIL212.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment

GOSPHIL214.name: Philosophy of Mind
GOSPHIL214.contribution: o What is the nature of consciousness? o What explains the identity of selves over time? How have different philosophical traditions thought about this issue? o Can the mind be explained in neurobiological terms? o Are large language models conscious? Can they ever be? o What can we learn from dream states about conscious experience? o What can perceptual illusions teach us about our awareness of the world? o What are the differences between human and animal consciousness? These are some of the questions explored in the philosophy of mind, an important field of philosophy since early modernity. The field has come to prominence and maturation in the past decades alongside advances in the scientific study of the human mind, research on animal minds, and innovations in computing. In this course, we will focus both on important work from the history of the field and on contributions from recent scholarship. We shall begin with exploration of the nature of selves and personal identity, looking at historical sources in the Western tradition, contemporary debate, as well as the theory of the self in Buddhist thought. Detailed discussion of approaches to the mind-body problem, a key issue in the philosophy of mind, will follow. Additional topics to be examined in the course include: the possibility of intelligent and conscious machines, animal minds, dream states, the significance of transformative experiences, and the impact of novel technologies on the ways we experience the world. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSPHIL214.topics: Persons and personal identity; Psychological and narrative theories of identity; Buddhist non-self; Split-brain cases and self-knowledge; Behaviourism; Physicalism and functionalism; Mind-body problem; Content externalism and internalism; AI intelligence and consciousness; Virtual reality; Dreaming and perception; Transformative experience; Value of conscious experience; Animal minds

GOSPHIL313.name: Free Will, Time & the Self
GOSPHIL313.contribution: Investigates concepts of free will, the role of luck and openness of the future. Explores relations between free will, time and the self across multiple modules and contemporary debates. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSPHIL313.topics: Free will and fatalism; Foreknowledge and determinism; Compatibilism and rival theories; Moral responsibility; Greek and Indian accounts of agency; Scientific perspectives on free will; Addiction and the self; Moral luck; Games and agency; Value capture; Reality and experience of time; Time and physics; Temporal asymmetries and bias; Time, action and selfhood

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: In the course Introduction to Political Philosophy we shall examine the views on the nature of man, of society, and of political authority held by a number of influential Western thinkers. By the means of their particular political theories, the thinkers in question certainly intended to contribute to the solution of problems affecting the communities they were part of and their time. We shall look at the intellectual presuppositions of their theories and compare the problems they intended to solve, as well as their solutions, with the most significant actual political problems, the perception the general public opinion has of them and our current solutions. In particular, we shall focus on the authors’ justification for the existence and organization of political power. The course aims to provide a comprehensive introduction to the nature, characters, and purposes of each of the various political theories examined, from classical antiquity to today. To achieve this goal it is designed as informative and critical. Students are expected to master a number of relevant items and to assess form and quality of the influence that certain political theories have had, and may still have, on present day politics. In the attempt to determine whether there are ‘perennial’ political problems and features, students are expected to constantly compare past and present, and to find out what are the possible connections between empirical and normative political science. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSPOLI111.topics: Society, rights and political authority; Classical political thought; Sovereignty and political realism; Enlightenment and revolution; Liberalism and conservatism; Feminism; Nationalism; Socialism and communism; Empire, race and decolonization; Welfare state and libertarianism; Neoliberalism; Justice

GOSPOLI311.name: European Union Politics
GOSPOLI311.contribution: This course introduces you to the European Union, a body politic that has been characterized as diverse as Unidentified Political Object, an unimperial empire as well as a superstate. Whatever its nickname , the EU is as political as any other body invested with public authority. For political scientists this means that it is vital to understand its functioning and to see where power is exercised and how various state and non-state interests try to get their preferences turned into policies. In the first part of the course we outline key actors, institutions and decision -making rules and show how political scientists have employed various ways to study EU politics and policy- making. Students will engage in Navigating the EU exercises that show them EU politics in the making and the sources to be used for that. In the second part of the course we will more directly examine the clash of interests through a group based research project where you study a legislative dossier and the interaction between interest groups and Members of the European Parliament, using the E Us transparency register . A key focal point in this analysis concerns the relative power of business interests vis a vis other interests in EU - decisionmaking and assessing what this implies for the legitimacy and effectiveness of EU - policies. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSPOLI311.topics: European integration; EU institutions and decision rules; EU legitimacy and democracy; Public opinion; Parties and European Parliament; Interest representation and lobbying; Agenda setting; EU legislation and implementation; MEP roles and committee behaviour; Political ideology and amendments; Policy salience

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: Peace and Conflict Studies is an interdisciplinary field that explores the causes, consequences, and potential solutions to both violent and nonviolent conflicts. Its goal is to understand the complex factors that contribute to conflict, the dynamics of violence, and the strategies for achieving lasting peace. The field encompasses insights from history, sociology, political science, international relations, and law, among other disciplines . This course introduces the field by examining and assessing multi ple theories of conflict and peacebuilding in the context of ongoing and past conflicts at regional, national and international levels. Peace and Conflict Studies is not only interdisciplinary but also shaped by diverse analytical perspectives. Some approaches emphasize structural inequality , clashing ideologies, and others focus on humiliation, historical wounds, and identity -based grievances, particularly in colonial or postcolonial contexts. Each lens draws attention to different forms of evidence and different peacebuilding strategies. As a result, this course demonstrates the importance of adopting a holistic approach that includes in ternational, institutional, and state -led elements, as well as cultural, interpersonal, and bottom-up actions led by civil society. The course uses “Travelling Concepts” as a tool for critically applying an interdisciplinary perspective. Students will compare how “justice,” “truth,” or “reconciliation” are mobilized in legal vs. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSPOLI313.topics: Conflict theories and structural violence; Identity and historical grievances; Colonialism and forced migration; International peace and security; Humanitarian law and human rights; Positive, negative and hybrid peace; Local peacebuilding; Frozen conflicts; Counterterrorism and rule of law; Transitional justice; Gender and conflict; Development and peacebuilding; Reconciliation, arts and religion; Global South perspectives; Travelling concepts and researcher positionality

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: Similar to their quantitative counterparts, qualitative researchers ask basic, but demanding, questions before they start making any enquires, e.g. What is truth? What is reality? What is knowledge? Why do we want to conduct research? What do we want to get out of it? In contrast to quantitative studies, however, qualitative researchers are less interested in numbers, trends and generalisations. Instead, they are keen to explore the messiness of social processes: what motivates people to take actions, how people make sense of their world, and how politics, history and cultures influence people’s thinking and actions. In this course, we will critically examine the four key stages of conducting qualitative research: (1) research design and preparation; (2) data collection and management; (3) data analysis and interpretation, and (4) research dissemination. Throughout the course, students are expected to take an active role – to form a research group and choose a research topic, to interrogate qualitative research theories and their own research experiences, and to critically reflect the research processes and students’ own positionality, biases and assumptions. At the end of the course, students will share their research findings and experiences with one another. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSSOCI212.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.contribution: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSSOCI215.topics: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: The course ‘GOSSOCI311 New Issues in Contemporary Sociology’ builds upon the topics covered in ‘GOSSOCI101 Introduction to Sociology’ and ‘GOSSOCI202 Modern Sociology’. Its primary goal is to familiarise students with significant debates in sociological theory from a global perspective. This edition of the course focuses specifically on the idea of civil society, examining topics such as solidarity, social capital, social trust, the public and civil sphere, and civil repair in modern societies. The first part of the course explores a critical approach to civil society, starting with Gramsci’s ideas, followed by Habermas’s ideas on the public sphere and Fraser’s critique. It will examine cases in the Global South, and we will watch and discuss a movie about the power of grassroots civil society. The second part focuses on Alexander’s work on the Civil Sphere, cases of civil repair in Latin America, and performances of solidarity with migrants along Europe's southern border. The final part will explore the decolonial critique of the classical approaches to civil society and the civil sphere. Alongside the theoretical component, the course also includes an empirical aspect. Students will select an NGO, voluntary organisation, or other Civil Society Organisation (CSO) to explore the concepts covered in the course and the challenges associated with the work undertaken by these organisations. Using a Community Engaged Learning (CEL) approach, students will observe and study an organisation throughout the semester to gain an understanding of its culture, impact, and challenges. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
GOSSOCI311.topics: Civil society; Social trust and social capital; Hegemony; Critical theory; Public spheres, digital publics and counterpublics; Solidarity and civil repair; Civil sphere; Social movements and intersectionality; Migrant solidarity; Civil society under authoritarianism; Decolonial critique; Public sociology

MCCCOMM111.name: The Art of Rhetorical Communication
MCCCOMM111.contribution: Tweets by politicians and celebrities. Social media conspiracy theories. Product advertising. Anti-war protests. Speeches about justice. These are all examples of rhetorical discourse. Both the internet and history books are full of examples of the relevance of the art of rhetoric, as are our daily lives. Plato defined rhetoric as the “art of enchanting the soul”, while Aristotle considered it the ability to “discover in any particular case, all of the available means of persuasion". Quintilian, on the other hand, simply considered rhetoric to be “the art of the good person speaking well”. Whatever the definition, mastering this art often involves more work than is often imagined; work that is at the core of this course. This course is a fundamentally a skills course, even if there is a significant amount of rhetorical history and theory. No effective standpoint can be formed, no supporting arguments found, no paper written, no presentation given, no textual analysis conducted without knowledge of how rhetoric works. Therefore, it is necessary for students to have a proper understanding of what rhetoric is and what it involves, and also how rhetoric can be applied consciously. This course offers the skills that students will need to be able to structure any future academic essay or future oral presentation in a clear, persuasive and academic way. The course starts by considering the Greek and Roman Western roots of rhetoric. It focuses on the canons of rhetoric applied to the three main types of argumentation, i.e. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCCOMM111.topics: Greek and Roman rhetoric; Deliberative, forensic and epideictic discourse; Logos, ethos and pathos; Invention, arrangement, style, memory and delivery; Argumentation and fallacies; Tropes and schemes; Stasis and enthymemes; Persuasive speech; Narrative and storytelling; Immersive educational communication

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.contribution: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCCOMM212.topics: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

MCCCOMM213.name: Rhetoric in Action
MCCCOMM213.contribution: To what extent can students on an undergraduate rhetoric course at a liberal art and science college empower a group of local primary school children to become more confident and more persuasive public speakers and debaters? This is the question that this course sets out to explore in this practice-based ‘Rhetoric in Action’ module. In this course, students will learn about the theory and practice of the public work of rhetoric. They will also learn about what Community Engaged Learning is and about how it will shape their roles during this course. After an introduction to these theories, the students will then be trained in several public speaking, debating and storytelling exercises that will build on what they have already learned in the 100-level rhetoric class. With their new didactic skills and knowledge, they will then design several innovative public speaking and debating exercises for the school children. Before the mid-term break, the teaching and learning space will shift from the UCR classroom to local school Magistraal. The students will then work with small groups of primary school children and their teachers. These children are sometimes from socio-economically disadvantaged groups and are aged between 9 and 12. The language of interaction will principally be Dutch, but English, and even Arabic, may come into play in certain cases. The UCR students will be teaching and training the school children in the different forms of public address that they have themselves designed. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCCOMM213.topics: Public work of rhetoric; Community-engaged learning and reciprocity; Public speaking and debate; Storytelling; Children's rhetorical confidence and civic participation; Rhetorical teaching and coaching; Cultural sensitivity; Collaboration with community partners; Experiential and reflective learning

MCCCOMM311.name: Persuasive Communication
MCCCOMM311.contribution: This third-year course on ‘persuasive communication’ in the connected realms of ‘science, society and sustainability’ will build on your existing knowledge of classical rhetoric and argumentation theory and look at persuasion mostly beyond the humanities in the fields of communication studies, social psychology and neuroscience. The course has several aims. The first is to make students aware of persuasion strategies that circulate in everyday social discourses. These discourses can be found in the domains of local politics, law, advertising, business, media and governmental institutions. Students will be introduced to new theoretical frameworks and models, such as framing, nudging, cognitive shorthands and the coactive model of persuasion. Simultaneously, they will learn about the importance of the ethics of persuasive communication in given public contexts. Ethical theories that we will explore will range from utilitarianism to universalism and from dialogic ethics to situationalism. The course will build towards a significant community engaged learning (CEL) element. This is the main aim of the course; namely, to get university students out of the classroom and into the real world of work and applied skills experience. This CEL aspect will mainly take place in the second half of the semester. Here, with their newly acquired persuasive communication knowledge and skills, students will help local institutions to address and solve both internal and external communication challenges that they currently have. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCCOMM311.topics: Persuasion models and psychology; Ethics of persuasion; Coactive persuasion; Verbal and nonverbal communication; Message framing; Argumentation; Cognitive shortcuts and nudging; Science and sustainability communication; Circular lifestyles; Community-engaged communication

MCCCOMM312.name: Creative Communication Laboratory
MCCCOMM312.contribution: Creative Communication Laboratory is an academic course that examines how meaning is produced through imagination, experimentation, and artistic practice. Creative work is studied and developed within a framework of critical reading, analytical discussion, and reflective writing. Communication is approached as a cultural and theoretical problem shaped by language, sound, rhythm, performance, and media. You will analyze how writers and artists use language to generate meaning beyond description, and how formal deviation operates as a deliberate, historically situated practice rather than error. The first part of the course focuses on poetry and performance as foundational practices. You will progress from traditional lyric forms to bent, strained, and experimental poetry, situating these practices within literary, historical, and cultural contexts. Class emphasizes rhythm, sound, imagery, voice, and embodiment, combining close reading with creative and analytical work. In this course, poetry is treated both as a genre and as a transferable set of strategies that cultivate formal control and precision. After Spring Break and the exam, the course turns to hybrid forms and independent creative projects. You will extend poetic methods into broader creative practices, including performative, sound-based, or digitally mediated work. Final projects may not involve singing, songwriting, or music performance, and sound-based work is permitted only when sound functions as a poetic, linguistic, or conceptual material. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCCOMM312.topics: Meaning and formal experimentation; Lyric poetry; Poetic sound and rhythm; Imagery and voice; Embodiment and performance; Constraint and formal deviation; Experimental poetry; Hybrid and digitally mediated forms; Creative process and revision; Aesthetic traditions and conceptual coherence

MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.contribution: This course provides a chronological overview of Western art history from the early Renaissance to the present. It emphasizes key paintings that define specific periods or movements, exploring the works and their creators in detail. The course also considers the impact of art institutions, markets, critics, and historiographers on the legacy of these masterpieces. Focusing on major stylistic movements in Europe and the Americas, the course lays the groundwork for advanced art history studies. It introduces essential tools for visual analysis and interpretation, fostering an understanding of how visual culture reflects historical contexts and societal values. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCHEAM111.topics: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.contribution: How does making things define human existence and societies, from their earliest beginnings to the end of antiquity and beyond? This course examines this question first, through the pragmatics of manufacture in relation to religious, social, and gendered identities, from Çatalhöyük (Türkiye) in 10.000 BCE and the region of Kush (Sudan) around 8.000 BCE, to classical Athens and Rome, and from the Harappan Valley to the Philippines. In every context we will explore the artefacts, their production and their makers. By exploring these, we can discover the story of the communities that made them. We will look at individual manufacturing techniques from settlements in different parts of the world, and how the objects made in (urban) communities could help people negotiate identity. We will look at the social and environmental impact of these crafts, and how technologies have helped shape social identity through the ancient world. The course has an experimental component where we design an educational activity surrounding an archaeological or ancient craft-related theme, for which a main requirement is that it involves a hands-on activity. Finally, we will explore how archaeological research methods can be used in contemporary settings. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCHEAM112.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology

MCCHEAM213.name: Greek Archaeology
MCCHEAM213.contribution: Explores the archaeology of community and democracy in early-democratic Greece, seeking ancient lessons on community decision-making. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCHEAM213.topics: The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the modern world.

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.contribution: This course examines key debates on modern art through a carefully selected range of themes and topics. A central focus is the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions. By exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies, students will gain insight into how art institutions shape public perception and understanding of modern and contemporary art. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCHEAM312.topics: Modernism and avant-gardes; Cubism and abstraction; Modern architecture and design; Figuration and Mexican muralism; Abstract Expressionism; Minimalism and Pop Art; Postmodernism and conceptual art; Photography, installation, performance and video art; Globalization and contemporary art; Authorship, originality and medium; Museums, curating and reception; Eurocentrism in art history

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.contribution: Literature is common ground. It is ground not managed wholly by commercial interests, nor can it be strip-mined like popular culture…There’s a lot of talk about the tame world versus the wild world. It is not only a wild nature that we need as human beings; it is the untamed open space of our imaginations. Reading is where the wild things are. Jeannette Winterson Why Be Happy When You Can Be Normal. London, Vintage, 2012, p.144 The course is an introduction into practical criticism and literary interpretation. It explores some basic issues of literary study starting from the questions: what is literature, why do we read it, and why do we study it? The course familiarises students with formal properties of a literary work, makes them aware of a constructed character of literary text, and opens discussion of literary value. It is based on a classic division into three major genres (fiction, poetry and drama), supplemented by contemporary non-fiction, and rudiments of film narration. The goal of the course is to provide students with basic critical terms, tools and techniques that will make them sensitive readers and enhance their appreciation of a literary work. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCLITR111.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation

MCCLITR212.name: Life & Travel Writing
MCCLITR212.contribution: The course is devoted to various forms of life narrative in literature and popular culture such as memoir, autobiography, diary, personal essay, travel narrative as well as blog. It prepares students to read and analyse them, and be sensitive to autobiographical modes in the media. Through this critical encounter with life storying students are encouraged to develop a critical awareness of the postmodern ‘culture of autobiography’ (Folkenflik, R. The Culture of Autobiography. Stanford UP, 1993). In the course, students will build up their writing, presentation and debating skills, and their critical self-reflection. They will be invited to prove their comprehension of crucial theoretical aspects of life narrative research referring to their own individual experience and applying their creative writing skills in order to produce structured personal narratives. With its broadly conceived approach to life narrative studied in the context of large cultural processes, the course ideally fits the paradigm of liberal arts. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCLITR212.topics: Autobiography and memoir culture; Fact, fiction and autobiographical truth; Autobiographical pact; Self and multiple identities; Individual and collective memory; Experience, embodiment and agency; Ethics and traumatic memory; Grief and disability narratives; Popular memoir and narrative technique; Digital self-presentation; Travel and spiritual self-fashioning; Migration, language and cultural identity

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.contribution: It is a researched fact that more than 50% of films have their literary originals. More than three-quarters of the American Academy Awards have been granted to films based on novels, short stories and dramas. There are plentiful examples of famous films based on no less famous literary texts, from the already hackneyed Pride and Prejudice, through Bridget Jones’ Diary, The Lord of the Rings, the Narnia cycle, A Passage to India, Batman, A Thousand and One Nights to Frankenstein, Dracula, Ninety Eighty-Four and Hamlet. This close relation between literature and film becomes even clearer when we realize that film is a text that tells a story. Keeping this in mind, in this course we will discuss various ways in which a literary original is translated on screen, tracing various links between literary and film narration, and various intertextual dimensions of film adaptation. The course offers instruction in a methodology of film analysis, building on students’ knowledge of literature, media and popular culture. As it studies manifold transactions between the adaptor, the critic and the viewers, it is vital to every student interested in literature, media, popular culture and journalism. Our first step is the basic formalist analysis of a literary text along with its plot, structure, character, setting, and a formalist analysis of the multi-track film (image, acting, music, sound effects) along with its “syntax” and “diction” which all contribute to its tone and themes. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCLITR311.topics: Literature-film relationships; Narrative and medium specificity; Fidelity debates; Cinematography and mise-en-scène; Editing, continuity and montage; Film music and sound; Intertextuality; Auteurism; Adaptation and heritage; Adaptation markets; Spectatorship and immersion

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.contribution: MCCMED111: Introduction to Film & Media provides you with a solid foundation in the study of film, while also introducing you briefly to media more broadly. The course begins by tracing the development of cinema from its earliest experiments to later artistic movements and innovations. This historical perspective helps you understand film not only as entertainment but also as an evolving cultural form that reflects and shapes society. At the same time, we focus on the elements of film form, such as narrative, cinematography, editing, and sound, which give you the vocabulary needed to describe and analyze how films work. Much of our attention is on film culture and analysis, since these provide the best starting point for further study in the field. Together, we examine and discuss influential examples, considering both their artistic qualities and their broader theoretical and political contexts. This approach allows you to see how films respond to social change while also experimenting with style and technique. In the final part of the course, we widen our perspective to take a short look at media more generally. By considering examples from television, streaming, and digital platforms, we make connections between film and the wider media environment and prepare the ground for more advanced courses in the cluster. Engagement with academic readings is another central part of the course. These texts present important concepts and debates that shape the study of film and media. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCMEDI111.topics: Film form and meaning; Cinematography, editing and sound; Mise-en-scène, narrative and performance; Early cinema; German Expressionism and Soviet montage; Classical Hollywood and European New Waves; Feminist film theory; Postcolonial media; Blockbusters; Television and digital platforms; Representation and spectatorship; Media convergence

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.contribution: Media Archaeology explores the cultural and material significance of pre-digital media technologies, such as cassette tapes, typewriters, and early printed books, and how they shaped the production, circulation, and preservation of knowledge. We will study these objects from multiple perspectives, combining close material analysis with broader historical and cultural interpretation. You will examine how physical properties such as weight, texture, and durability influence communication and memory. The course will include seminar discussions, critical reflections, and hands-on activities that encourage active engagement with obsolete media. Practical exercises may involve recording silence, identifying the sonic characteristics of cassette hiss, or investigating the design, use, and cultural impact of the Sony Walkman. Through these activities, we will learn to treat media as both historical evidence and lived experience, linking material form to cultural meaning. These media objects are chosen because they exemplify the theories and readings central to debates in media archaeology today. By the end of the semester, you will have developed analytical thinking, interpretive skill, and cultural awareness consistent with the aims of a liberal arts education. You will be able to explain how studying obsolete and pre-digital technologies informs our understanding of today’s media. No technical expertise is required, only curiosity and a willingness to work closely with media as physical and cultural artifacts. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCMEDI112.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura

MCCMEDI211.name: From T.V. to TikTok
MCCMEDI211.contribution: This course examines social history and everyday life through American mainstream media from the mid-twentieth century to the present. Its central premise is threefold. First, storytelling shapes how we understand the world. Second, who gets to tell the story matters. Third, media provides insight into the past, present, and constructions for possible futures. Engaging with narratives across a wide range of media, from television and film to podcasts and TikTok, supports this point. So does amplifying the voices of the silenced and treating viral moments, such as a Justin Bieber performance clip, as cultural snapshots that reveal contemporary values, anxieties, and desires. The course opens with fear, conformity, and identity, using The Twilight Zone (1959) and Black Mirror (2011–) as bookends of the same uneasy question: what does society do to the individual? Week two then draws from future foresight methodology to explore the question: what does society imagine for itself in the future? Who is centered and who left out of the imaginations? The course then turns to mediated constructions of "reality," placing competing versions of the same story side by side and asking who the narrative serves and who it harms. Case studies include the "Hollywood Indian" versus films written, directed, and acted by Native Americans. The juxtaposition exposes how the media both marginalizes and empowers. A parallel examination of disability representation contrasts the inspirational "disabled hero" trope with authentic portrayals by differently abled people themselves. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCMEDI211.topics: Media storytelling and power; American everyday life; 1950s television and conformity; Science fiction and social anxieties; Media futures and marginalization; Indigenous representation and self-representation; Disability stereotypes and visibility; Authentic voice and cultural agency; Future foresight and inclusive scenarios

MCCMEDI212.name: Media & the Environment
MCCMEDI212.contribution: Media and the Environment examines how environmental issues are represented and debated through visual and audiovisual media. You study how media shape the ways ecological problems are understood, felt, and acted upon. The course introduces key concepts such as the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested ideas of nature, and indigenous and postcolonial media. You use these concepts as analytical tools to examine how environmental meaning is produced across different media forms and cultural contexts. The main goal of the course is to help you analyze environmental media critically and precisely. You learn how film, photography, sound, and digital media make ecological processes, environmental risk, and human and nonhuman relations visible and intelligible. The course emphasizes close analysis of images, narratives, and aesthetic strategies, as well as comparison across media genres and historical moments. You also examine how media translate scientific knowledge and lived experience into stories, images, and affects that shape public understanding, sustainability discourse, and political judgment. Questions of agency, scale, temporality, and responsibility guide your analysis throughout the course. The course combines sustained reading with structured discussion and applied analytical work. You work with scholarly texts, media examples, and guided exercises, and you complete either a final analytical paper or a media-based project. This combination reflects the core idea of the course. Contribution is limited to the actual taught subject and assessment. No whole Maastricht module, research trajectory or professional equivalence claimed.
MCCMEDI212.topics: Environmental representation; Anthropocene; Animal representation and human-nonhuman relations; Deep time and ecological temporality; Biocentrism and environmental justice; Contested ideas of nature; Indigenous and postcolonial media; Ecological risk and scientific knowledge; Environmental affect and perception; Agency, scale and responsibility; Sustainability discourse

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.contribution: In this course we will discuss the development of the documentary form and discover various techniques used by documentary film makers. We start by tracing the documentary film from its origins (e.g. including the work of pioneer documentarians like Dziga Vertov and Robert Flaherty) to the present.
